question: Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje’i, the Chief Justice of Iran, has warned EU citizens that they will ‘will bear the consequences of the meaningless decision’ by EU Foreign Ministers to list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation.

The Iranian armed forces too have described the EU’s decision as ‘illogical, irresponsible and malicious’, as well as showing ‘blind submission to US politics and the Zionist regime’. At the same time, the President of the Iranian Parliament has stated that his country regards the armies of EU countries as ‘terrorist organisations’. 1.
How are European citizens being protected against threats issued in defence of a system that has orchestrated the killing of over 6 000 people and the arrest of over 45 000 people?
Has an official communication been sent to the EU system itself by the Iranian regime, or are these three statements simply to be seen as a means of manipulating EU citizens?

Does the Vice-President / High Representative know of any non-governmental organisations in the European Union that are currently advancing Iran’s interests under the guise of religious, educational, medical or humanitarian activities?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2026) The EU is aware of the referred statement attributed to the Chief Justice of Iran, which however has never been communicated via official channels. The EU has a comprehensive policy approach towards Iran and uses all tools at its disposal, including sanctions, to defend its citizens and interests.

On 16 March 2026, the Council adopted new restrictive measures against 16 individuals and three entities responsible for serious human rights violations, including prominent figures such as the Deputy Minister of Interior and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Commanders1. In addition, on 19 February 2026, the Council finalised the listing of the IRGC as a terrorist organisation2.

The regulation and supervision of non-governmental organisations operating on the territory of Member States fall primarily within the competence of the Member States, in accordance with national law and applicable EU law.
